hut-interior-wall-of-packing-cases.head: Inside the hut at Cape Evans, a wall of packing cases divided the officers from the sailors.
hut-interior-wall-of-packing-cases.body: The hut at Cape Evans was one long room, but Scott divided it into two parts. The dividing wall was made of wooden packing cases filled with stores, such as bottled fruit and other supplies. On one side lived the officers and scientists, in a space called the wardroom. On the other side lived the sailors, in a space called the mess deck, close to the kitchen. This arrangement copied life on a naval ship, where officers and men lived separately. Historians note that the division reflected the society of the time, with its clear ranks and classes. Even so, the wall was not a barrier to friendship. Men from both sides worked together every day and shared the same food and dangers. The packing case wall had another advantage. As the winter went on and stores were used, the cases slowly emptied. The men joked that the wall was getting thinner every week.

wardroom-long-table-acetylene-lamps.head: Scott had a small private corner in the hut, with a bunk, a desk and photographs of his family.
wardroom-long-table-acetylene-lamps.body: As leader of the expedition, Scott had a small cubicle at one end of the wardroom. It held a bunk, a small desk and a shelf of books. On the wall were photographs of his wife, Kathleen, and his young son, Peter. Next to his cubicle, Wilson and the second in command, Lieutenant Edward Evans, had their own spaces. The wardroom was lit by acetylene lamps, which gave a bright white light. A long table stood in the middle, where the officers and scientists ate and worked. Historians know about the layout from plans, photographs and diaries. Scott spent many hours at his desk, writing his journal, planning the journey to the Pole and working out supplies. Even so, he was often seen walking through the hut and talking with the men. Ponting's photograph of Scott writing at his desk is one of the best known images of the expedition.

crowded-bunks-saddles-clothes-hut.head: The most crowded corner of the hut was nicknamed the Tenements.
crowded-bunks-saddles-clothes-hut.body: Five men shared a small cubicle in the wardroom. They were Bowers, Oates, Cherry-Garrard, the doctor Edward Atkinson and the ponies' assistant Cecil Meares. Their space was so crowded and untidy that it was nicknamed the Tenements, after the crowded housing of poor city districts. Bunks were squeezed tightly together, and clothes, boots, saddles and equipment were piled everywhere. Oates kept pony gear there, and Bowers stored all kinds of useful items. Historians know about the Tenements from diaries and from Ponting's photographs, which show the men sitting on their bunks. Even so, the men were proud of their corner. They made jokes about its untidiness and enjoyed one another's company there. Cherry-Garrard later wrote warmly about the friendships formed in that small space. The Tenements became a symbol of the closeness of the men who lived and worked together through the long Antarctic winter at Cape Evans.

hut-kitchen-stove-cook-bread.head: The expedition's cook, Thomas Clissold, baked fresh bread almost every day.
hut-kitchen-stove-cook-bread.body: At the sailors' end of the hut was a large iron stove, where the cook prepared meals for the whole team. The cook was Thomas Clissold, a young man who had worked in kitchens before joining the expedition. He baked fresh bread nearly every day and prepared meals from tinned food, seal meat and penguin. He was also inventive. He built small gadgets, including one that rang a bell when the dough had risen. Historians know about him from diaries, which praise his cooking. Even so, his job was hard. Cooking for twenty-five hungry men in a small space, with limited ingredients, required great skill and planning. Clissold also took part in some sledge work. Later in the expedition, he was injured in a fall while posing for one of Ponting's photographs. Afterwards, he lived for many years in New Zealand, where he died in 1963.

hut-dinner-table-tins-jam-tea.head: The men's meals at Cape Evans included seal meat and penguin as well as tinned food.
hut-dinner-table-tins-jam-tea.body: The expedition brought large amounts of tinned and preserved food from Britain, including meat, vegetables, fruit, jam, biscuits, butter and cocoa. To add fresh food and to prevent scurvy, a disease caused by a lack of vitamin C, the men also ate seal meat and penguin. Historians note that scurvy had been a serious problem on earlier expeditions, and fresh meat helped protect against it. According to diaries, the men had mixed feelings about penguin meat. Some found it delicious, while others described its taste as like beef that had been soaked in fish. Seal liver was considered a special treat. Meals followed a regular pattern, with breakfast, lunch and dinner at set times. Even so, the food was generally good and plentiful. On special occasions, such as birthdays, the cook prepared extra dishes. Mealtimes were among the most important social moments of each day in the hut.

pianola-gramophone-corner-hut-lamplight.head: The hut at Cape Evans had a pianola, a piano that could play itself, and a gramophone.
pianola-gramophone-corner-hut-lamplight.body: The expedition took a pianola and a gramophone to Antarctica. A pianola is a piano that can play itself, using rolls of paper with holes punched in them to control which notes are played. The gramophone played records, including popular songs and classical music. Historians know about the music from diaries, which mention the pieces the men enjoyed. Music helped the men relax, especially during the long winter darkness. Evenings often ended with music, and some men had favourite records that they asked for again and again. Even so, the choice of music sometimes caused friendly arguments. Some men preferred classical pieces, while others liked music hall songs. The pianola and gramophone were treasured possessions. In such an isolated place, they brought a feeling of home. The sound of music in the warm hut, while the wind howled outside, was something many men later remembered with great affection.

darkroom-red-light-photographs-drying.head: Herbert Ponting had a small darkroom in the hut, where he developed his photographs.
darkroom-red-light-photographs-drying.body: Ponting was given a small darkroom at one end of the hut. It was a tiny space, about two metres by two metres, where he developed glass plate negatives and printed photographs. He slept there too, on a narrow bunk. The darkroom was lit by a dim red lamp, because ordinary light would spoil the photographic plates. Historians note that the darkroom was one of the warmest places in the hut, since it had to be kept warm for the chemicals to work properly. Ponting worked there for many hours, carefully developing his pictures. Even so, the work was difficult. Water had to be made from melted ice, and chemicals had to be kept from freezing. Yet the results were remarkable. Ponting's photographs and films are among the most important records of the expedition. Many of his glass plates and prints survive today in museums and archives, including the Scott Polar Research Institute in Cambridge.

scientists-laboratory-corner-microscope.head: The scientists had their own working corner in the hut, with microscopes, instruments and specimens.
scientists-laboratory-corner-microscope.body: Part of the hut was set aside for scientific work. The scientists had benches with microscopes, instruments, books and specimens. The biologists examined small sea creatures under microscopes. The geologists studied rocks and fossils. The physicist and meteorologist kept instruments that recorded the weather and the Earth's magnetism. Some instruments had pens that drew continuous lines on paper, recording changes in wind and pressure day and night. Historians consider the scientific records of the expedition to be of great value. The weather data is still used by scientists studying the climate of Antarctica. Even so, the work was demanding. Instruments had to be checked regularly, often in freezing conditions outside. The meteorologist George Simpson was nicknamed Sunny Jim. His careful records helped scientists understand Antarctic weather for the first time. The scientific corner was a busy place, where work continued throughout the long winter at Cape Evans.

ponies-in-snow-stables-blankets.head: The expedition's ponies were small, tough horses brought from Manchuria in northern China.
ponies-in-snow-stables-blankets.body: Scott decided to use ponies to help pull sledges on the journey south. He had seen them used by Ernest Shackleton on an earlier expedition. Nineteen ponies were bought in Manchuria, a region in northern China, and brought by ship to New Zealand. They were small, strong and used to cold weather. At Cape Evans, they lived in a stable built along one side of the hut. Historians have long debated Scott's choice of ponies. Ponies are heavy and sink into soft snow, and they need large amounts of fodder, which must be carried. Norwegian explorers preferred dogs, which are lighter and can eat seal meat. Even so, Scott believed ponies could carry heavy loads across the ice shelf. The ponies were given names, and the men became fond of them. Some ponies were gentle, while others were difficult. Looking after them was hard and constant work.

cavalry-officer-brushing-pony-stable-lam.head: Captain Oates criticised the quality of the ponies but cared for them devotedly.
cavalry-officer-brushing-pony-stable-lam.body: Oates was put in charge of the ponies because of his experience with horses in the army. When he first saw them in New Zealand, he was unhappy. Many were old or in poor condition, and he felt they were not suitable for the journey. He wrote in letters home that they were the worst collection of animals he had ever seen. Even so, he worked tirelessly to keep them healthy. He spent many hours in the stable, feeding, grooming and exercising them. When a pony was ill, he stayed with it through the night. Historians note that Oates's care for the ponies earned him great respect. The men appreciated his dry humour and his honesty. He was nicknamed the Soldier and sometimes Titus. In the stable, he would sit and smoke his pipe among the animals. His devotion to the ponies is one of the most remembered parts of the expedition's story.

white-pony-gentle-young-man-snow.head: Each pony had its own name and character, from wild and difficult to calm and gentle.
white-pony-gentle-young-man-snow.body: The men gave the ponies names, and diaries describe their different personalities. Some ponies were calm and easy to handle. Others were wild and stubborn. One pony, called Christopher, was so difficult that several men were needed to hold him while he was harnessed. Another, called Jimmy Pigg, was known for being gentle. Cherry-Garrard led a pony called Michael, and Bowers led one called Victor. Scott had a favourite named Snippets. Historians know about the ponies from diaries, letters and photographs. Even so, the ponies' story is a sad one. None of them survived the expedition. Some died during the depot journey, and the rest were used on the first part of the journey to the Pole, after which they were killed for food, as planned. The men who had looked after them wrote with sadness about losing them. Diaries show how attached they had become to these hardworking animals.

siberian-sled-dogs-curled-snow.head: The expedition's sled dogs came from Siberia and slept outside in the snow, even in blizzards.
siberian-sled-dogs-curled-snow.body: The expedition brought more than thirty sled dogs from Siberia, in eastern Russia. They were chosen by Cecil Meares, who had travelled widely in Asia. A young Russian dog driver named Dmitri Girev came with them to help. The dogs were thick-coated and hardy. Unlike the ponies, they lived outside, sleeping in the snow even during blizzards. They curled up tightly, covering their noses with their tails to stay warm. Historians note that Scott did not fully trust dogs for the main journey to the Pole, partly because of difficulties on his earlier Discovery expedition. Even so, the dogs proved useful in many ways. They pulled sledges on several journeys and helped carry supplies. They were fed on seal meat and dried fish. The dogs had names and personalities too. Diaries describe their noisy fights, their excitement at mealtimes and their great strength when pulling heavy loads.

adelie-penguins-curious-ice-edge.head: Adélie penguins lived near Cape Evans, and the men enjoyed watching their busy lives.
adelie-penguins-curious-ice-edge.body: Adélie penguins are the most common penguins on the coast of Antarctica. They are small, black and white, with white rings around their eyes, which make them look surprised. They live in large colonies, called rookeries, where they build nests of small stones. Historians note that the expedition's scientists studied them carefully. The surgeon George Murray Levick, a member of the Northern Party, spent a whole summer observing a large colony and later wrote a book about their behaviour. Even so, some of his observations were thought too shocking to publish at the time and were only made public a century later. The men found the penguins entertaining. Diaries describe them stealing stones from each other's nests, chasing intruders and tumbling into the sea. They were not afraid of people and would often walk right up to the men. Watching them was one of the great pleasures of the summer.

weddell-seal-sleeping-sea-ice-sun.head: Weddell seals lived under the sea ice near Cape Evans and could be heard calling beneath it.
weddell-seal-sleeping-sea-ice-sun.body: Weddell seals are large seals that live farther south than any other mammal. They spend much of their lives under the sea ice, keeping holes open by scraping the ice with their teeth so they can breathe. On sunny days, they lie on the ice to rest. Historians know from diaries that the men often heard the seals calling under the ice. Their calls are strange, musical sounds, with trills, whistles and chirps. Some men described them as singing. Scientists today know that Weddell seals use these calls to communicate. Even so, seals were also an important source of food for the expedition. Seal meat was eaten by the men and fed to the dogs, and seal blubber was used as fuel. The seals were not afraid of humans, since they had no natural enemies on land. The men were often impressed by how calmly the seals lay on the ice.

snow-petrels-white-birds-over-ice.head: Snow petrels, small pure white seabirds, flew over the ice near Cape Evans.
snow-petrels-white-birds-over-ice.body: Snow petrels are among the most beautiful birds of Antarctica. They are completely white, except for black eyes and a dark beak. They live farther south than almost any other bird, nesting in cracks in rocks and cliffs, sometimes far inland. Historians note that the men of the expedition often saw them flying over the ice and sea. Wilson, who was an expert on birds, painted them. Diaries describe them as looking like ghosts or snowflakes as they flew past. Even so, the men saw many other birds too. Skuas, large brown seabirds, often stole food and attacked penguin nests. Giant petrels and other species visited the coast. The scientists collected and studied the birds, adding to knowledge of Antarctic wildlife. Snow petrels have a special defence. When threatened, they can spit a strong-smelling oil at an attacker. The men learned to treat them with respect.

emperor-penguin-tall-golden-neck-ice.head: Edward Wilson wanted to study the eggs of the emperor penguin, the largest penguin in the world.
emperor-penguin-tall-golden-neck-ice.body: The emperor penguin is the largest penguin in the world. It can stand more than a metre tall and has a golden patch on its neck. Unlike other birds, it breeds in the middle of the Antarctic winter. The male holds the egg on his feet, under a fold of skin, and keeps it warm for about two months in total darkness and extreme cold. Historians note that in 1911, very little was known about emperor penguins. Wilson believed that their embryos, the young birds developing inside the eggs, might help scientists understand how birds had evolved from reptiles. At that time, some scientists thought that an embryo's development repeated the history of its species. Even so, collecting emperor penguin eggs meant travelling in the middle of winter to the nearest known colony, at Cape Crozier. It would mean a journey of more than one hundred kilometres in darkness and terrible cold.

depot-flag-cairn-snow-plain-evening.head: Before the winter, the men laid down a large store of supplies called One Ton Depot.
depot-flag-cairn-snow-plain-evening.body: In early 1911, before the winter began, Scott led a journey south across the Ross Ice Shelf to lay depots. A depot is a store of food and fuel left along a route, to be used on a later journey. The largest depot was called One Ton Depot, because it held about a ton of supplies. It was marked with a cairn of snow and a flag, so that it could be found again. Historians note that One Ton Depot was placed further north than Scott had originally planned. The ponies were struggling, and Scott decided not to push them further. This decision later became important, because the depot lay about eleven miles beyond where Scott and his companions would be trapped on their return. Even so, the depot journey was difficult. Several ponies died, and some men had a narrow escape when sea ice broke up. The men returned to Cape Evans as winter approached.

last-sunset-before-winter-ice-hut.head: In April 1911, the sun set at Cape Evans, and it did not rise again for four months.
last-sunset-before-winter-ice-hut.body: Because Antarctica lies so far south, it has months of continuous daylight in summer and months of continuous darkness in winter. At Cape Evans, the sun set for the last time in late April 1911. It would not rise above the horizon again until late August. Historians note that the men marked the last sunset with a sense of occasion. Some gathered outside the hut to watch the sun disappear behind the mountains. Diaries describe the beautiful colours of the sky in the final days of light. Even so, the darkness was not complete at first. For several weeks, there was twilight around midday. Later, the darkness deepened, and only the moon, stars and southern lights brightened the sky. The men prepared carefully for the long night. They had food, fuel and plenty of work to keep them busy. The winter at Cape Evans had begun.

aurora-australis-green-curtains-hut.head: During the polar night, the men often watched the southern lights, called the aurora australis.
aurora-australis-green-curtains-hut.body: The aurora australis, or southern lights, is a natural display of light in the sky near the South Pole. It happens when particles from the sun strike the Earth's atmosphere. The lights appear as glowing curtains, arcs and rays, usually green, sometimes red, pink or purple. In the long winter darkness at Cape Evans, the men often saw the aurora. Historians know about these displays from diaries, which describe them in detail. Wilson painted them, and scientists recorded their shapes and times. Even so, the scientists did not fully understand what caused the aurora. Today, scientists know much more about the connection between the sun and the lights. The men found the aurora beautiful and moving. Some stood outside for long periods despite the cold, watching the lights ripple and change across the sky. Scott described them in his journal as a scene of indescribable beauty and wonder.

hut-breakfast-porridge-morning-lamps.head: In the winter darkness, life in the hut followed a regular daily routine.
hut-breakfast-porridge-morning-lamps.body: To stay healthy and cheerful during the winter, the men followed a strict daily routine. They woke at the same time each morning and had breakfast at eight o'clock. Porridge, bread, butter, jam and tea were common breakfast foods. After breakfast, each man went to his work. Scientists studied their specimens and recorded data. Others repaired equipment, made sledges and clothing, and cared for the ponies and dogs. Lunch was at one o'clock, and dinner was at half past six. Historians note that Scott believed a regular routine was essential. On earlier expeditions, long periods of darkness had caused depression and illness. Even so, the routine was not too strict. Sunday was a day of rest, with a church service led by Scott. Every day, someone took turns as night watchman, keeping the stove going, checking the instruments and watching over the hut while the others slept.

men-leading-ponies-moonlight-sea-ice.head: During the winter, the men exercised the ponies in moonlight and sometimes had to find their way through blizzards.
men-leading-ponies-moonlight-sea-ice.body: Even in the darkness of winter, the ponies needed daily exercise. On clear days, the men led them across the sea ice near the hut, often by the light of the moon. Diaries describe the beauty of these walks, with the ice glowing silver and the mountains faintly visible. Historians note that the weather could change suddenly. Blizzards swept in with little warning, bringing strong winds and blowing snow. In a bad blizzard, it was impossible to see more than a few feet. The men sometimes used ropes and lines to find their way between the hut and nearby instruments. Even so, there were dangerous moments. On one occasion, Scott himself was lost for a short time while walking near the hut. Men were sent out to search for people who had not returned. The blizzards reminded everyone how dangerous the Antarctic could be, even close to home.

men-reading-playing-chess-hut-evening.head: Several evenings a week, the men gave lectures to each other on their special subjects.
men-reading-playing-chess-hut-evening.body: To pass the long winter evenings, the men organised a programme of lectures. Three evenings a week, one member of the expedition gave a talk on his own area of knowledge. Wilson spoke about penguins and birds. Ponting showed photographs of his travels in Japan and India. Oates gave a talk about the care of horses. Scientists spoke about geology, physics and weather. Scott talked about his plans for the journey to the Pole. Historians know about these lectures from diaries, which describe them as interesting and lively. Even so, not every lecture was easy to follow, and some led to long discussions. On other evenings, the men read books from the hut's library, played chess and cards, wrote diaries and letters, and listened to music. The lectures helped the men learn from each other and fill the long hours of darkness with something interesting.

handmade-newspaper-sealskin-cover-table.head: The men produced their own newspaper during the winter, called The South Polar Times.
handmade-newspaper-sealskin-cover-table.body: During the winter, the men wrote and illustrated a newspaper called The South Polar Times. It had first been made on Scott's earlier Discovery expedition. Cherry-Garrard was the editor during the Terra Nova expedition. Members wrote stories, poems, articles and jokes, and Wilson contributed paintings and drawings. Each issue was typed and bound by hand. The covers were made from materials found at the base, such as wood from packing cases and sealskin. Historians note that only one copy of each issue was made, and the men took turns reading it. Even so, it was read eagerly by everyone. The newspaper gave the men a way to share their humour and creativity. Some contributions were anonymous, and the men enjoyed guessing who had written them. Original copies survive in museums and archives. A facsimile edition was later published, so that readers could see what the men had made.

midwinter-feast-flags-table-celebration.head: On the twenty-second of June 1911, the men celebrated Midwinter Day with a feast.
midwinter-feast-flags-table-celebration.body: Midwinter Day, around the twenty-second of June, is the darkest day of the year in Antarctica. After it, the days slowly begin to grow lighter, and the sun's return comes closer. For Antarctic expeditions, Midwinter Day became an important celebration, like a second Christmas. At Cape Evans in 1911, the men decorated the hut with flags, and the tables were laid with special food. There was a dinner of seal, roast beef, plum pudding, mince pies and other treats. Historians know about the celebration from diaries and photographs. Bowers made a Christmas tree from ski sticks, decorated with candles and small gifts. There were speeches, toasts and songs. Even so, the evening was also a time for reflection. Many men thought of their families at home. The celebration lifted everyone's spirits. It was a sign that the darkest part of the winter was over.

three-men-hauling-sledge-dark-lantern.head: In June 1911, Wilson, Bowers and Cherry-Garrard set out in the darkness to collect emperor penguin eggs.
three-men-hauling-sledge-dark-lantern.body: On the twenty-seventh of June 1911, just after Midwinter Day, three men left Cape Evans on a remarkable journey. Edward Wilson, Henry Bowers and Apsley Cherry-Garrard set out to walk to Cape Crozier, about one hundred kilometres away, to collect emperor penguin eggs. They pulled two heavy sledges themselves, without ponies or dogs. They travelled in almost complete darkness, using candle lanterns and moonlight to find their way. Historians consider this one of the hardest journeys ever made in polar history. Cherry-Garrard later described it in his book, which took its title, The Worst Journey in the World, from this experience. Even so, the three men had volunteered for the journey. Wilson believed the eggs were scientifically important, and the others were willing to go with him. The journey also tested food, clothing and equipment that would later be used on the expedition's journey to the Pole.

polar-night-snow-plain-stars-moonlight.head: On the winter journey, temperatures fell below minus sixty degrees Celsius.
polar-night-snow-plain-stars-moonlight.body: The cold during the winter journey was extreme. Temperatures fell to around minus sixty degrees Celsius, and at times even lower. Historians note that these were among the lowest temperatures ever experienced by people travelling at the time. Cherry-Garrard described how their breath froze immediately and fell around them. Their clothes froze so stiff that they could not bend them. Sleeping bags became filled with ice, and it took hours each night to work their way into them. Even so, the three men kept going. The surface of the snow was so cold that it felt like sand, and the sledges were very hard to pull. Some days, they covered only a few kilometres. The darkness made everything more difficult. They often could not see where they were going and stumbled into crevasses, deep cracks in the ice. The journey to Cape Crozier took nearly three weeks.

small-tent-lantern-glow-dark-snow.head: Despite terrible conditions, the three men on the winter journey remained kind and patient with each other.
small-tent-lantern-glow-dark-snow.body: Cherry-Garrard later wrote about the remarkable friendship among the three men during the winter journey. Despite the cold, the darkness and the exhaustion, they never quarrelled. They remained polite and kind to one another, even when they were suffering badly. Historians often quote Cherry-Garrard's admiration for his two companions. He described Wilson as calm and wise, and Bowers as tireless and cheerful. Every night, they set up their tent and cooked a meal of pemmican, a mixture of dried meat and fat, with biscuits and hot drinks. They used a small stove that burned paraffin. Even so, the effort of each simple task was enormous. Their fingers were frostbitten, and every movement was slow. Yet they shared the work and looked after one another. Cherry-Garrard believed that their friendship and good manners were the reason they survived. Their small tent became a home in a hostile world.

stone-hut-rocks-ice-ridges-twilight.head: At Cape Crozier, the three men built a small hut of stones, and a storm blew away its roof.
stone-hut-rocks-ice-ridges-twilight.body: When the three men reached Cape Crozier, they built a small hut of rocks and snow on a hillside, with a canvas roof. They hoped it would be a base while they visited the penguin colony below. Historians note that they named the place Oriana Ridge, after Wilson's wife. Even so, disaster struck. A violent blizzard hit, and the wind tore their tent away. Then the canvas roof of the stone hut was ripped off. For more than a day, the three men lay in their sleeping bags in the open, with snow blowing over them. They believed they might die. When the storm ended, they searched the area and, by great luck, found the tent caught among rocks some distance away. Without it, they could not have survived the journey back. The ruins of their stone hut can still be seen at Cape Crozier today, more than a century later.

emperor-penguins-huddle-winter-twilight.head: The three men reached the emperor penguin colony and collected five eggs.
emperor-penguins-huddle-winter-twilight.body: Before the storm, Wilson, Bowers and Cherry-Garrard made their way down to the emperor penguin colony. It lay below high ice cliffs, on the sea ice. Getting there in the darkness was very hard, and they had to climb through ridges of broken ice. Historians know from Cherry-Garrard's account that they found about one hundred emperor penguins, far fewer than expected. Some of the birds were holding eggs on their feet. The men collected five eggs, carrying them carefully in their mittens. Even so, two of the eggs broke on the way back, when Cherry-Garrard stumbled in the darkness. Wilson prepared the remaining three eggs to preserve the embryos. He also collected some penguin skins and blubber. For a short time at the colony, the three men forgot their suffering. Seeing the great birds in their winter home was an extraordinary experience. No one had ever seen this before.

three-tired-men-arriving-hut-dawn.head: The three men returned to Cape Evans on the first of August 1911, and their three eggs are now kept in London.
three-tired-men-arriving-hut-dawn.body: The journey back to Cape Evans was as hard as the journey out. The three men were exhausted, frostbitten and suffering from lack of sleep. Their sleeping bags were so frozen that they could hardly use them. Historians note that they returned to the hut on the first of August 1911, after five weeks away. The other men were shocked by their appearance. Their faces were scarred by the cold, and they could barely move. Even so, they recovered after some days of rest and warmth. Scott wrote that it was the hardest journey ever made. The three emperor penguin eggs were later taken to the Natural History Museum in London. Scientists examined the embryos, but the results did not provide the answers Wilson had hoped for. The eggs are still kept at the museum today. Cherry-Garrard's account of the journey has become one of the most famous stories of exploration.
